Welcome to Boston’s Freedom Trail. Originally designed in the 1950s, the Freedom Trail is an iconic symbol of Boston. Its red brick line snakes through some of the oldest parts of this City, leading visitors to notable historic sites in the Downtown, North End, and Charlestown neighborhoods of Boston. The trail introduces visitors to Boston's storied, complicated, and multi-faceted history. While many sites are primarily recognized for their role in the American Revolution, all the sites on the Freedom Trail have stood as the backdrop of subsequent social, political, and religious movements, controversies, and challenges. Learn More Park Street Church The church was founded in 1809, at the corner of Park and Tremont Streets, atop the site of Boston’s town grain storage building, or granary. Designed by Peter Banner, the 217 ft. steeple of Park Street Church was once the first landmark travelers saw when approaching Boston. Learn More Boston Latin School Site/Benjamin Franklin Statue Boston Latin School, founded on April 23, 1635, is the oldest public school in America. It offered free education to boys - rich or poor - while girls attended private schools at home. Until the completion of the schoolhouse in 1645, classes were held in the home of the first headmaster, Philemon Pormont. A mosaic and a statue of former student Benjamin Franklin currently marks the location of the original schoolhouse. You are here Home › Cemeteries › Granary Burying Ground Last updated: 2/20/26 Granary Burying Ground The Granary Burying Ground, located at 120 Tremont Street in downtown Boston, is the city's third oldest cemetery. The Granary Burying Ground was the third burial site in Boston Proper, established in 1660. Town officials set aside part of what was then the Boston Common for burial space to help alleviate overcrowding in the near-by King’s Chapel Burying Ground. First, the space was known as the South or Common Burying Ground, and then the Middle Burying Ground (after the opening of Central Burying Ground). The Granary Burying Ground took its present name in 1737 when a granary, a small building used to store grain, was moved to the site presently occupied by the Park Street Church. The Granary Burying Grounds contains approximately 2,345 gravestones and to

rst, the space was known as the South or Common Burying Ground, and then the Middle Burying Ground (after the opening of Central Burying Ground). The Granary Burying Ground took its present name in 1737 when a granary, a small building used to store grain, was moved to the site presently occupied by the Park Street Church. The Granary Burying Grounds contains approximately 2,345 gravestones and tombs, although it is estimated that over 5,000 people are buried at this site. The grave markers are predominantly slate. The gravestones’ original configuration was rearranged into straighter rows over the years to accommodate both nineteenth-century aesthetics and the modern lawnmower. Underground burial crypts (tombs) line the entire perimeter of the site. These crypts are small rectangular rooms, made of brick or stone, designed to hold multiple burials, which were frequently owned by families. Older underground tombs are found in the center of the site. Many well-known people from American history are buried at this site. Visitors will find the graves of three signers of the Declaration of Independence: Samuel Adams, John Hancock, and Robert Treat Paine; patriot and craftsman Paul Revere; James Otis, a Revolutionary orator and lawyer; the five victims of the Boston Massacre, including Crispus Attucks, considered to be the first casualty of the American Revolution; and Peter Faneuil, benefactor of the famed downtown Boston landmark. Go to Shop The History of 263 Summer St A Building That Helped Shape the City Long before it became home, 263 Summer Street played a working role in Boston’s industrial rise. Constructed in 1905 by the Boston Wharf Company, the building was part of a network of warehouses, offices, and manufacturing spaces that defined Fort Point as one of the city’s most productive districts. Designed by architect Morton D. Safford , whose work helped shape the neighborhood, the building was created for durability, efficiency, and longevity—qualities that still define it today. From the start, this was a place built to last. Summer Street & “Wool Row” At the turn of the 20th century, Summer Street was known as “Wool Row” —the customer-facing edge of Boston’s wool and textile trade. Merchants, manufacturers, and logistics operations lined the corridor, connecting industry to the waterfront, the rail system, and the rest of the city. Early tenants reflected that energy and scale, including the U.S. Army Depot Quartermaster , Windrum Shoe Manufacturing , and the Boston Wool Trade Association . This building wasn’t ornamental—it was essential. Built on Resilience The story goes deeper than the brick walls. Fort Point itself was built on land created from the debris of Boston’s Great Fire of 1872 —a city-scale reset that led to a stronger, more modern Boston. That cycle of reinvention is literally beneath your feet, embedded in the character of the district, and carried forward by the buildings that rose from it. The Sig

t was essential. Built on Resilience The story goes deeper than the brick walls. Fort Point itself was built on land created from the debris of Boston’s Great Fire of 1872 —a city-scale reset that led to a stronger, more modern Boston. That cycle of reinvention is literally beneath your feet, embedded in the character of the district, and carried forward by the buildings that rose from it. The Sign That Never Went Dark Rising above Summer Street is the iconic red neon “Boston Wharf Co Industrial Real Estate” sign—a fixture that has guided pedestrians and commuters for generations. Officially recognized within Fort Point’s landmark guidelines, the sign has been described as a beacon marking the passage from downtown into Boston’s industrial age. Over the years, it has been repainted and reinterpreted by local artists, reinforcing its role as more than signage—it’s a cultural marker. While much around it has changed, the sign remains, anchoring the building to its origins. A New Chapter Begins More than a century after its construction, 263 Summer Street enters its next era as part of Boston’s office-to-housing transformation—preserving what makes the building significant while reimagining what it can be. The exterior remains unmistakably historic. Inside, the spaces have been fully modernized for contemporary living, with clean lines, warm materials, and thoughtful layouts that respect the building’s industrial bones without replicating the past. This isn’t history frozen in time—it’s history, adapted. Still Standing. Still Evolving. Today, 263 Summer Street stands as a rare balance: a building with memory, character, and presence—redefined for the way Boston lives now. What began as a place of work has become a place to live. What was built for industry now supports community. And what has endured for more than a century continues to move forward. Contact Have a question or want to schedule a tour? Operated by the Boston Sparks Association since 1983. Step through the door of the historic firehouse at 344 Congress Street and onto the apparatus bay floor that now houses a museum dedicated to the history of the nation’s first and oldest professional fire department. Featuring historic artifacts, interactive exhibits, and plenty of educational opportunities, this museum offers a glimpse into the past that is both inspiring and unforgettable. Conveniently located between and within walking distance of Boston’s Financial District and the popular Seaport District, the museum is a must-see for history buffs, fire service enthusiasts, and children of all ages. 344 Congress Street, South Boston Open Saturdays 10am–4pm • Free Admission Directions and Parking What You’ll See at the Museum Vintage Former Firehouse —Built in 1891 to house Engine Companies 38 and 39 —Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1987 —Still contains working telegraph fire alarm bell and tape register connected to an active circuit on the City’s telegraph fire alarm system —Museum displays a hand-made, scale cutaway model of the building as it appeared in the early 20th century Antique Fire Apparatus —“Hand Tub” water pumper built in 1792 by an apprentice to Paul Revere —“Hand Tub” water pumper built in 1851 and used by the former City of Charlestown (prior to annexation by Boston) —1882 steam engine (former Boston Fire Engine 26 / Engine 50 / Engine 38) —1926 American la France pumper (of Horseheads, New York; resembles former Boston Fire Eng

evidence.quote: Museum. No museum ticket is required to visit Abigail’s Tea Room, making it a great stop for both museum guests and visitors exploring the area. Abigail’s Tea Room offers a wide assortment of food and beverage options, including a tea tasting experience where visitors can drink the 5 teas involved in the Boston Tea Party. Guests hoping to continue their learning after finishing their interactive museum tour will be thrilled to find that Abigail’s Tea Room & Terrace also holds several historical exhibits, artifacts, and text panels, as well as historic table games to play as you sip your tea. Is the museum wheelchair accessible? Yes. The museum is wheelchair accessible, including exhibit spaces and restrooms. Please note that given our unique nautical environment, movement through the site involves gangways, ramps, and some tight spaces. Our museum building includes an elevator for your convenience. While we have two ships on-site, only 1 is fully ADA- accessible. Our ship Eleanor is fully ADA accessible with ramp access to the top deck and video displays to convey content and information regarding the spaces below decks. Tours that board the Eleanor begin at either the top or bottom of the hour. For better wheelchair access and accessibility please book a tour at one of these times.
